opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think we're anywhere close to the limits of the transformer for robotics, and the reason is that the bottleneck right now isn't the architecture, it's the data.

If you look at language models, the transformer had the entire internet to chew on. In robotics we don't have an internet-scale corpus of robot actions. You can't scrape motor control data from Wikipedia. So when people ask whether the transformer has hit a wall for robot foundation models, my first reaction is that we haven't fed it enough to find out where the wall is.

The way I think about it, there's a data pyramid. At the top you have real robot data, collected through teleoperation. It's the highest quality and the most directly useful, but it's incredibly expensive, because you're bounded by humans and hardware, roughly 24 hours per robot per day. In the middle you have simulation, where you can run things thousands of times faster than real time and randomize physics and visuals. At the bottom you have the huge pile of internet video and human demonstrations, which carries a lot of priors about how the world works but has no action labels. The real game is figuring out how to blend all three, and the transformer is a great substrate for that because it's so flexible about what tokens you put into it.

That said, I wouldn't claim the architecture is final. A few things could push us beyond it. One is the dual-system idea: a slower, deliberate vision-language model doing reasoning and planning, paired with a fast, reactive policy running at high frequency for motor control. That isn't throwing out the transformer, but it does change how you compose these models. Another is that diffusion and flow-matching action heads have turned out to be really important for producing smooth, multimodal action distributions, which a vanilla next-token objective doesn't handle as gracefully. Latency and real-time control on edge hardware also put pressure on the architecture in ways chatbots never have to deal with.

So my honest assessment is that the transformer is still the right workhorse, and the frontier is in data strategy, the training recipe, and system design around it. When we've saturated the data and the scaling curves start to flatten, that's when I'll seriously worry about the architecture. We're just not there yet. Physical AI is maybe where language models were a few years before GPT-3, and there's a lot of runway left.

r001.rationale: It says transformers are “nowhere close to the limits” for robotics and that the architecture has not yet been tested at sufficient scale.

r002.rationale: It says robotics lacks an internet-scale corpus of robot actions and that motor-control data cannot be scraped from sources like Wikipedia.

r003.rationale: It mentions flexible tokens and a next-token objective, but does not present learning from robot action tokens by next-word prediction as a hypothesis still being tested.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think the transformer itself is the bottleneck, honestly. People love to ask "is attention dead," but when I look at what's actually limiting robot foundation models today, almost none of it is the architecture.

The real constraint is data. Language models got to drink from the ocean of the internet. Robots don't have an internet of actions. There's no Wikipedia of motor torques. So the question I ask is not "has the transformer hit a wall," it's "have we hit the wall on how much embodied experience we can feed it." And the answer there is that we're nowhere close. We're in the GPT-1 era for robotics in terms of data scale.

That said, there are a few places where I do watch for architectural limits. One is latency. A humanoid needs to run control at tens or hundreds of hertz, and a giant autoregressive transformer is not naturally built for that. So you see this split emerging: a slow "System 2" model that reasons about the scene and the task, built on vision-language transformers, and a fast "System 1" policy that actually drives the joints, often something smaller, sometimes a diffusion or flow-matching head, sometimes a lightweight transformer. That's not the transformer failing, that's us learning where to put it.

The second thing is continuous, high-dimensional action spaces. Tokenizing actions the way we tokenize text is a bit of a hack. It works surprisingly well, but I think the right output head for a 50-degree-of-freedom body is still an open question.

And the third is memory over long horizons. Doing laundry is a 20-minute task with lots of partial observability. Context windows help, but I'm not convinced pure attention is the final answer for an agent that needs to remember what it did an hour ago in the physical world.

So my honest assessment: the transformer is still the best general-purpose substrate we have, and the frontier is not replacing it. It's simulation at scale, real-world data flywheels, and figuring out the right interfaces between reasoning and control. If a better architecture comes along, great, but it won't matter until we solve the data problem. Right now the limiting reagent is experience, not attention.

r001.rationale: The response says the transformer is not the current bottleneck, calls it the best general-purpose substrate, and says the frontier is not replacing it.

r002.rationale: It says robots lack an “internet of actions” and “Wikipedia of motor torques,” identifying the lack of online motor-control data as the data constraint.

r003.rationale: It says action tokenization resembles text tokenization and that the output head remains an open question, but does not describe learning from action tokens as analogous to next-word prediction or frame that hypothesis as still being tested.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think we have enough evidence to say transformers have reached their limits in robotics. Robotics is still very constrained by data. So if a model isn’t performing well, is that an architecture problem, or is it because we don’t have enough diverse, high-quality interaction data? Those are hard to disentangle.

The way I’d assess it is to look at scaling: as we increase data, compute, and model size, do we keep getting better generalization to new objects, new environments, and new tasks? And we need to measure that on a real robot, in closed loop. Predicting the next action accurately on a recorded dataset isn’t the same as recovering when you drop something or when an object moves unexpectedly.

There are also practical constraints, like latency and how you maintain memory over a long task. Those may motivate changes to the architecture. But I’d separate ‘a vanilla transformer isn’t the complete robotics system’ from ‘transformers have hit a fundamental ceiling.’ You can build a system around a transformer with memory, perception, and control operating at different timescales. I think there’s still a lot of room to explore before we can make that stronger claim.

r001.rationale: The response says there is not enough evidence to conclude transformers have reached their limits and that more exploration is needed, but it does not clearly state that they have not yet been pushed to their architectural limits.

r002.rationale: It describes robotics as constrained by data, but does not attribute the bottleneck to a lack of downloadable motor-control action data on the internet.

r003.rationale: It does not present learning from robot action tokens as analogous to next-word prediction in text or describe that idea as a hypothesis still being tested.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think we’ve seen enough evidence to say transformers have reached their limits for robotics. Robotics has a very different data situation from language. We have an enormous amount of text on the internet, but we don’t have an equivalent internet of robots interacting with the physical world.

So if a robot model struggles, we have to ask: Is the architecture the bottleneck, or is it the amount and diversity of experience? Does the training objective actually teach the model what it needs to control a robot? Those are different questions.

The way I would assess it is through controlled scaling experiments. Increase the data, increase the compute, and measure performance on new objects, new environments, and longer tasks. Look at how reliably the robot recovers from mistakes, too. A compelling demo is very different from a system that succeeds consistently.

There are real challenges around latency, memory, and reasoning about physical dynamics. We may need additional structure or hybrid architectures. But before declaring a fundamental limit, I’d want to see that better data and better training have stopped producing meaningful gains. I don’t think we’re there yet.

r001.rationale: The response says there is not enough evidence that transformers have reached their limits for robotics and that it would be premature to declare a fundamental limit.

r002.rationale: It notes that there is no internet-scale equivalent of robots interacting with the physical world, but does not identify the bottleneck specifically as a lack of downloadable motor-control action data.

r003.rationale: The response discusses training objectives generally, but does not present robot action-token learning as analogous to next-word prediction or as a hypothesis being tested.
